segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples had watched him pray for years, and watched him come back from it different. So one morning they asked him for the thing they wanted most. Teach us how to do that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he gave them a prayer. And the first word of it was not Lord, and it was not God. It was the word a small child uses.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He taught them to walk up to God and call him Father. And then, to show them what kind of Father he meant, he told a story about a man banging on a door in the middle of the night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: People travelled at night there, because the daytime heat could kill you. So a friend really could turn up at midnight, starving — and you did not send him away. Feeding a guest was a duty the whole village shared.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So a man opens his door at midnight to a friend who has walked all day. Then he looks at his own shelf, and there is nothing on it. Not a crumb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he picks up his little clay lamp and walks out into a sleeping village, toward the one door he knows still has bread behind it.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him,

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Friend, lend me three loaves; for a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Notice who he is asking for. He is standing out there in the dark, begging for bread he will not eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the other side of that door, a village house was one room. The whole family slept on one platform under one blanket, behind a heavy bar. Getting up meant waking every child in the house.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is a no. And it is not a lazy no. That is a tired man with sleeping children and a real reason.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the man outside does the thing nobody expected. He knocks again. Louder. Shutters bang open up the street. Dogs start barking. And he keeps knocking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The word Luke uses here shows up nowhere else in the whole New Testament. Most Bibles turn it into the word persistence. It does not mean persistence. It means shamelessness. He was not too proud to look like a fool.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went for enough bread to feed one man. He came home with an armful. And notice why. The neighbour did not get up because they were friends. He got up because the man outside would not stop asking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in a dark house at midnight, a tired stranger ate a meal he never knew somebody had fought for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Here is where almost everybody gets this story wrong. People hear it and think God is the man behind the door. Annoyed. Asleep. Somebody you have to wear down.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is the opposite of what he said. The neighbour is not a picture of God — he is the contrast. If even a worn-out man behind a barred door will get up for you in the end, what will your Father do, when he was never asleep at all?

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the Greek, none of those is a one-time act. Every one of them means keep coming back.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he asked them: if your son asked for bread, would you put a rock in his hand? If he asked for a fish, would you hand him a snake? An egg — a scorpion?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every pair is a lookalike — a river stone the size of a flat loaf, a scorpion curled pale and round like an egg. A father handing his hungry child a counterfeit. Not one of you, he said, would ever do it.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You already know how to be good to your kids — and you are not half as good as he is. That is the whole argument: God does not have to be worn down. He was never asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man in the story was knocking on a door with somebody asleep behind it. You are not. Whatever you quit asking for — too small, too late, too much — the light in that house is already on. And the best thing he has to give was never bread. It is himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man at the door was not asking for himself, and he was not too proud to look foolish. What would you ask God for tonight, if you knew for certain he was awake?
